“The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, ‘literature’] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = “with”) the trends of life… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, “that which co-exists with hita [welfare]”. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, “Art for artʼs sake,” cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement “Art for artʼs sake” is not acceptable; rather we should say, “Art for service and blessedness.”… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

The range and scope of short stories are exactly the same as those of plays, but short-story writers must know the technique of presenting a long story concisely. Suspense is equally effective in short stories as in plays; dramatic skill is essential for the writer of those short stories which come in the category of sketches, because a sketch holds an intermediate position between a story and a play.”

In the unique and superb interpretation of sáhitya, literature, in terms of “Art for service and blessedness” given above, the author has provided eternal guidance to all those related to the world of literature. With the basic objectives set by the author, literature with all its branches, including plays and short stories, can truly build up an ideal and just society, which is the demand of the day.

Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (“The Practice of Art and Literature”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1) quoted from above. But he did not stop there. Advancing further, he translated his words into actions, creating a direct example in the form of his own literature, marked by his natural ease and aptitude. Thus we get a great series named Sarkarʼs Short Stories in fourteen parts. In June 1985, the first Bengali fourteen-part set was published under the authorʼs direct guidance. In January 1990, the English Sarkarʼs Short Stories Part 1 was published. Since then, there has been a persistent demand from our esteemed readers for the publication of all the parts. In response to that we are extremely happy to present to the readers now Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 1-3 in one volume. Genuine and sincere efforts are going on to publish all remaining parts within the next year. We fervently hope to fulfil this objective with the cooperation of all concerned.

All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast domain of linguistics and philology which touched also on history, geography, medicine, science, art, religion, spirituality, philosophy, etc. Such books included Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá (eight parts) and Shabda Cayaniká (twenty-six parts). Like most great authors, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar is a consummate storyteller, thus he used in those books a seemingly inexhaustible supply of anecdotes, personal experiences and interesting as well as educative references, in order to capture the readerʼs interest. And it is mostly those stories that have been excerpted to constitute the present book. Thus it is natural that in the stories contained in the present book, we will find, either at the beginnings of those stories or as footnotes, relevant references to the linguistic and other subjects of the original books. In this way the stories retain the authenticity of the original books. Apart from the books mentioned above, some stories are from a volume of the authorʼs childrenʼs literature series – namely, In the Land of Hat́t́amálá.
In the interest of accuracy, the authorʼs explanations of certain Sanskrit, Bengali and other terminologies have all been retained in full.
Source references for all material in the book are provided at the end of this publisherʼs note.
Footnotes by the translators have all been signed “–Trans.” Unsigned footnotes are those of the author.

Many readers are concerned that the authorʼs discourses, as published, should adhere as closely as possible to the precise wording the author used in speaking. For this reason, in the case of discourses given originally in English, the editors do not alter pronouns and other terms which the author in his lifetime considered “common-gender” words. As the author once said, “You know, ‘man’ is not only masculine gender, ‘man’ is common gender also. ‘Man is mortal’ – here ‘man’ means both male and female.”

The author was a natural advocate of womenʼs rights and on at least one occasion indicated that “lopsided justice” in language should be eliminated at some future date. In keeping with his guideline and with current trends, it is our policy in the case of translated discourses (where the published wording will necessarily be that of the translators) to use gender-neutral language.

Square brackets [ ] in the text are used to indicate translations by the editors or other editorial insertions. Round brackets ( ) indicate a word or words originally given by the author. When round brackets follow an English word or phrase and contain the equivalent Bengali word or phrase, it should be understood that the English words represent the English translation, while the contents of the brackets are the original Bengali words provided as extra information for the reader.

The author used a particular shorthand for explaining the etymologies of words. Under this system, a minus sign (–) follows a prefix, and a plus sign (+) precedes a suffix. Thus ava – tr + ghaiṋ = avatára can be read, “the root tr prefixed by ava and suffixed by ghaiṋ becomes avatára.”

The people of Ráŕh [land of laterite soil; a territory mostly in West Bengal, stretching from the west bank of Bhagirathi River to the Parasnath Hills] engage in serious philosophical exercises as much as they engage in light-hearted play; they are full of life – with laughter, amusements, dance, song, wit and humour (rága and rauṋga). They are sociable and prefer to remain in each otherʼs company and in a cheerful mood (khos mejájii) in a gathering. Though burdened with poverty, they invite people for meals. They serve what they themselves eat – rice, black gram (biŕi in Ráŕhii Bengali), baŕi-posta [dumplings made of pulse, flavoured with poppy seeds], curry and pumpkin (d́iḿlá in Ráŕhii Bengali). They are not inhibited in their behaviour due to their poverty. They are not shy to say clearly what ought to be said. Here is an example of the straightforwardness of the people of Ráŕh: ( 1 )
A judge asked a very simple, illiterate Ráŕhii karśaka ( 2 ) [farmer], “Well, you say that the land is yours; can you tell me how many embankments ( 3 )there are on the land?”
The illiterate farmer could not answer that question. He sat looking up into the air. The judge said, “What in the world are you looking at?”
The farmer replied, “Well, my lord, you have been sitting in judgment in this room for a long time. Now, without looking up, can you say how many beams and girders there are in the ceiling?”
The judge said, “Who tutored you to say this?”
The farmer replied, “No one, I spoke for myself. In my other statements, I was tutored by the lawyer. Now, I said just the right thing, and you should give just the right judgment.” ( 4 )

Such is the simplicity of the people in Ráŕh. So in the rural life of Ráŕh, there is no end to festivals and no shortage of ingredients for merry-making. Inexpensive and common decorations are an integral part of life in Ráŕh, but they have never been allowed to stand in the way of the simple lifestyle of the Ráŕh people.
1981, Kolkata
from "Ráŕh 27 – Social Life of Ráŕh"

[[In grammar, first the vyásvákya [original words used in expounding a word] has to be determined correctly in order to determine the samása [compound word]. In other words, the actual meaning of the word should be revealed and not merely the implied or "understood" meaning. Otherwise it would not be possible to determine the samása.]] In this context, a story comes to my mind.

Once, a lioness had given birth to four cubs in a London zoo (ciŕiyákháná in Bengali). A censor officer prepared a press release and sent it to his superior for approval. It read, “A lioness has given birth to four cubs in a zoo in London.”

The superior officer was unhappy with the note. He said, “Why did you mention London? The information may be of help to the enemy!” So he corrected the sentence in this manner: “In a certain zoo in a certain city in England, a lioness gave birth to four cubs.”
When he forwarded the revised note to his own superior for confirmation, he was told, “A zoo in England would automatically mean the London zoo. This news is going to benefit the enemy.”
The press release was, therefore, changed further as follows: “In a certain zoo in a certain city of a country in the world, a lioness gave birth to four cubs.”
When he sent the note to his higher authority, he said, “The zoo in London is the best in the world. It has no peer. Hence mention of the word zoo would mean the London zoo”.
Hence he revised the note further in this manner: “At a place in a certain city of a certain country of the world a lioness gave birth to four cubs.”

The note was then sent to an even higher officer for approval. Reading it, he was livid with rage, “Do you not have any grey cells? A lion always signifies the British Lion. Hence, even the mere mention of the animal will spill the beans.”
He corrected the note thus: “In a certain place in a certain city of a country in the world, an animal gave birth to four cubs.”

This final draft of the press release then reached the topmost officer of the department. He was clearly displeased and remarked with great irritation, “I am tired of trying to hammer some sense into you people! Is it ever prudent to reveal a specific number? The actual number has to be exaggerated or reduced or sometimes even left unspecified according to the need.”
Therefore, the note finally read as follows: “In a certain place in a city of a certain country in the world, a certain animal gave birth to a few cubs.”

As I was telling you, when you are investigating what are the [[original words constituting]] a compound word, do not follow this policy of the censor department. It will not help you in understanding the word.
1983, Kolkata
from "Compound Words (Discourse 18)"

It should be kept in mind that in linguistics, edicts are always correlated with interdicts. “Yes” and “No” are complementary to each other. One cannot exist without the other. This is true in every sphere. In philology, we therefore have to keep in mind that even if we forget the primary edicts, the exceptions (apaváda in Hindi) are to be remembered as much as possible.

For example, in English, if there is a single vowel before a single consonant, then when an inflection is added to the consonant, it is doubled. “Fit” in that case becomes “fitting”, “fitted”, etc. But there are exceptions as well – like “benefit” where, even with the addition of an inflection, the “t” is not doubled.

I knew of two men who were proficient in the English language. One was Mr. S.P. Banerjee and the other was Mr. G.C. Banerjee. The latter, in a letter to his Kolkata office from Tatanagar, had used two “t”s in the word “benefit”. When the letter reached Mr. S.P. Banerjee, he called the other Banerjee and said, “My dear Gour, why did you double the ”t“?”

Mr. G.C. Banerjee, in a superior manner, replied, “Sir, you left your studies quite a long time back. I believe you have forgotten your grammar. When a single vowel is used before a single consonant, the letter is doubled when an inflection is added after the consonant. This is the edict. So I used a double ‘t’.”

The humourist in Mr. S.P. Banerjee replied, “Whatever the edict is, I think you have done the right thing by doubling the ‘t’. You had written the letter from Tatanagar. On the way to Kolkata, it would have to pass through Kharagpur, a dangerous place where train robberies are frequent. Even if the dacoits stole a ‘t’, the other ‘t’ would still be there, would it not?”
31 July 1983, Kolkata
from "Language and Dialect – 1 (Discourse 7)"

In every city of every country in the world, there exist the sycophants who excel in servile flattery without getting paid for it. These unpaid sycophants are even more subservient than those who get paid for being one. Let me tell you a story.

It was about forty to forty-five years ago. There lived a well-known medical practitioner in the city who was called Arun Banerjii (surname changed). Dr. Banerjii was a reputed physician with a good practice. He earned plenty and gave away more in charity. No needy person had ever been turned away by this humble (amáyik), benevolent man. As if by a natural process, a circle of sycophants had formed around the good doctor. There were a few very experienced and capable flatterers in this group, although the doctor never encouraged anyone.

Dr. Banerjii was very fond of his mother. He always told others, who did not know, that his mother, a widow, had struggled through many adversities to raise him single-handedly. Recently, his mother had fallen ill. The doctors who examined her had given up hope of her survival. They said plainly, “At the most, she may survive for two more days.” Dr. Banerjii took utmost care of his mother.
Somehow, the news reached the sycophants. They came running in hordes, weeping profusely, and crowded inside the doctorʼs house.
Some said, “Oh, what a pity! We never thought that our beloved auntie would leave us like this.” Others said, “How shall we endure our beloved auntʼs departure? This is terrible!”
Dr. Banerjii said in a low voice, “Please allow my mother to die first.”

Yet others had arrived already dressed with a napkin tied around their waists, carrying bamboo sticks, large, thick and heavy knives, and ropes for the last journey of the lady. They said, “Our beloved aunt was an exceptionally virtuous lady. We have never come across such a pious woman even in books and tales.”
Once again, Dr Banerjii said softly, “Please allow my mother to die first.”

The sycophants who had heard the news late came prepared to make up for the delay. Some of them wailed, “The holy woman that she was, the merit her soul had gained would surely enable her to attain the abode of Shiva (Shivaloka).” Others were too excited and declared, “I saw her observing fast (ekádashii) for all forty days last month.” Still others said, “Why should she go to shivaloka and subsist on boiled sunned rice and ghee? She deserves to reach the celestial abode of Viśńu (Vaekuńt́ha) and have rich, sumptuous food there.” Some others were heard to say, “An astrologer once predicted to me that our aunt had a place earmarked for her in the abode of Krśńa (Golokdháma).”
Dr. Banerjii had had enough. He said a little irritably, “All of you, please carry on. I have to go inside.”
The sycophants rose in unison and clamoured, “Oh, do not bother about such things! What are we here for? We have come ready to take her to the cremation ground.”
In order to extricate himself from them, Dr. Banerjii said, “All of you stay here. I have to go to the bathroom.”
The gathering of servile flatterers cried out, “Why should you bother with such small things? Have you not just lost your mother? We shall go to the bathroom on your behalf.”
Dr. Banerjii collapsed helplessly in his seat. He did not know what to do.

Once upon a time, a drastic change was noticed in the pronunciation of Eurasian (Anglo-Indian) names. The corruption was partly natural and partly wilful with the intention of projecting oneself to others as being non-Indian in origin.

Hence, Basu was transformed to Bose, Mitra to Mitter, Ghosh to Gas and Dutta to Dutt. The surname Paul is common to some Englishmen, so Bengali Pal became Paul, Das became Dias; Bandyopádhyáya, or Báṋŕujye, came to be known as Banerji or Bonerji; Mukhopádhyáya, or Mukhujye, as Mukherji; and Chat́t́opádhyáya, or Cát́ujye, as Chatterji.

Once, someone from the Anglo-Indian community in Allahabad came to our city. The man was smart and intelligent. From the complexion of his skin or his manners, it was impossible to distinguish him from a thoroughbred Englishman. No one would like to call him an Anglo-Indian. He could speak broken Bengali. He said, “I have interacted with Bengali people for a long time and picked up a smattering of their language. I am Kánis Gas.”

However, Gas Sáhib [a way of addressing an Englishman] was seen to buy native vegetables like the thor [the spathe of a banana tree before it shoots from the stem], figs, mocá [banana flower], ridge gourd (jhiṋe) etc. from the market. He used to say, “A sister of mine learnt some recipes from a Bengalee family. She cooks a very delicious and unique dish with jhiuṋe [ridge gourd] and posta [poppy seeds].”
In due course an aunt from Allahabad came to visit me. She asked me, “One of my cousins has recently been transferred here. Have you met him?”
I said, “Only one person has come here from Allahabad recently, but he is not a Bengalee! He is an Anglo-Indian named Kánis Gas.”
My aunt exclaimed, “That is the one! He is my cousin, Gańesh Ghosh, but calls himself Kánis Gas. He actually hails from Garbeta Village in Midnapore District where my maternal uncle resides.”
Varńa Vicitrá Part 3

One who is entrusted with the responsibility of management is known as the “manager”, which is adhyakśa in Sanskrit. A manager is sometimes mistakenly called an adhikárii, which is grammatically incorrect. Adhikárii is actually a Bengali synonym for “proprietor”. Have you heard the story of the adhikárii?

This man managed an open air drama group (yátrá). He pocketed three-quarters of the entire profit and distributed only one-quarter to his employees. The employees were therefore very dissatisfied. However, they kept their grievances to themselves because the adhikárii played all the lead roles himself. He knew all his lines by heart; hence, the prompter backstage was never able to cause him any trouble.

Unfortunately once did he forget certain parts of his lines. He was in the role of Rama. He was supposed to call out loudly, “Hanuman, Hanuman, where art thou?” But, as bad luck would have it, the name Hanuman eluded his memory. The sly (ghoŕel ( 1 )) adhikárii looked at the prompter and concert party and sang, “Who was the one who set fire to Lanka?”
When it came to slyness, his staff were not lagging too far behind. They sang in reply, “How would we know, who get only a quarter share?”
The proprietor had no other alternative but to bow his head like the legendary Vindhya Mountains. He sang, “We shall share fifty-fifty from now on.”
The staff chorused happily, “Oh, he was the great warrior, son of the wind god, Hanuman.”
That night, the opera (giitábhinay ( 2 )) was a resounding success.
Varńa Vicitrá Part 4

chapterTitle: It Is Not What You Think

t: Epilepsy is a neurological disease. When a young boy or girl suddenly has an unexpected experience, his or her nervous system and mind are sometimes subjected to intense pressure. If the pressure is too much to tolerate, epilepsy may set in.
chapterTitle: It Is Not What You Think

t: Let us assume, for instance, that a boy of twelve or fourteen looks up to someone whom he thinks is free from any addiction. When he suddenly discovers that in real life the man is an inveterate drunkard, his previous image of the man is shattered as if with a hammer blow. It may cause epilepsy in the boy.
chapterTitle: It Is Not What You Think

t: Suppose a certain boy was under the impression that he came from a good family Then, one fine day, he found thai he did not have any such pedigree. The shock may make him an epileptic.
chapterTitle: It Is Not What You Think

t: An unforeseen pressure on the nerve fibres of an epileptic person or a sudden soothing experience on the nerves may cause a relapse. Let us suppose that such a person feels the urge to urinate but is unable to find a suitable place to do so. When finally they are able to relieve themselves, such a profound sensation of pleasure engulfs the nerves that epilepsy can strike them during the act itself!
chapterTitle: It Is Not What You Think

t: When an epileptic suffering from extreme heat suddenly takes a dip in a lake or a river, the deep sense of comfort may trigger the disease and cause that personʼs death by drowning. Thus, a person with epilepsy should not be allowed to venture alone for a bath in a pond or river.
chapterTitle: It Is Not What You Think

t: Speaking of epilepsy, I recall an incident. Once, a habitual addict of Krishnanagar had drunk to his gills and spent the night lying in a drain. A gentle breeze at the break of dawn and the touch of cold water flowing down the drain brought him to his senses. He opened his eyes and found a crowd looking down at him. He felt just a shade bashful and closed his eyes. [[He]] looked up again after a few moments. He discovered his sonʼs father-in-law (vaeváhika) gazing at him from the crowd which made him feel very ashamed.
chapterTitle: It Is Not What You Think

t: The degree of his shame increased further. “My sonʼs father-in law must have guessed what happened! What will happen now,” he mused. Looking at him [sonʼs father-in law], he exclaimed in a casual voice, “it is not what you think, my friend! It is only epilepsy.”

chapterTitle: It Is Not What You Think

t: In your individual lives, you must have noticed frequently the practical expression of the power of dyotamáná [a stage of speech expression where one cannot find the appropriate words to explain the idea – when the shakti of speech reaches the region of the anáhata cakra] a number of times. Let me tell you a few incidents which may seem very familiar to you.

There was once a formidable (jáṋdrel ( 1 )) farmer (karśaka ( 2 )), whose name was Shrii Dantavikásh Nyájsarvasva (a surname). Dantavikásh had gone to his in-lawsʼ house for a visit. There, he was treated with great affection and care (yatna-átti – the word átti is derived from átmiyatá, meaning, kinship.)

The mother-in-law (shashru-thákuráńii ( 3 )) of Dantavikásh had prepared a princely feast (jámái bhog) for him. She had specially cooked a few hot sugarcane pancakes (guŕ-pit́he) in strained oil. Dantavikásh lost no time in eating them – it could be called a direct passage from the dish to the tongue! Munching on one, Dantavikásh felt like he was in seventh heaven. The pleasure he derived from the second one robbed him of his power of speech. Somehow, he managed to say, “Can I have a few more?” His mother-in-law replied happily, “Why a few! I shall cook a few dozen at once.”
Dantavikásh devoured all the pancakes and then asked respectfully, “What are these called?” The mother-in-law replied, “Madhupiśt́akii in Sanskrit. In Bengali, these are called guŕpit́he.”

Afterwards, Dantavikásh set out for his own village. He was not literate and so he could not write down the name of the delicious food. Lest he forget, he marched military style and chanted guŕ-pit́he, guŕ-pit́he, guŕ-pit́he instead of left-right, left-right, left-right.

This reminds me of an old experience. It was 1943, the days of the British Ráj .At that time, I was a trainee in the army. Scottish Highlanders, who were very capable soldiers, taught us how to parade. The only bad thing about them was their pronunciation as it was mostly unintelligible to Indians. We copied their style of command like a parrot – “illeft-áit, illeft-áit, illeft-áit”. Some of us were totally illiterate – they could not fathom what was said and so a special method of training was devised for them.

Some khaŕ [straw] was tied to their left foot and bicháli [a large grass plant which is used as cow fodder and for making ropes] to their right foot. Instead of “illeft-áit”, the command for them was khaŕ-bicháli, khaŕ-bicháli, khaŕ-bicháli. Once they became used to it, they were taught “illeft-áit”.

Dantavikásh was rhythmically marching towards his village muttering guŕ-pit́he, guŕ-pit́he, guŕ-pit́he. He came across a wide drain in the way. Dantavikásh gathered his energy and crossed it with a big leap. Alas! The name guŕ-pit́he vanished from his memory. Undaunted, Dantavikásh marched on uttering a new command, “what did I eat, what did I eat, what did I eat.”
Upon reaching home, he said to his mother, “Cook me the food I ate at the in-lawʼs house.”
His mother replied, “What shall I cook if you do not tell me what it was?”
Dantavikásh repeated over and over again, “What did I eat, what did I eat, what did I eat.”

The mother could not make out what her son wanted. Losing his patience, Dantavikásh kicked up a big row. The neighbours came running .The mother wailed, “Learned men were right! A fool is unendingly miserable. Rather than have a fool as a son, it is better not to have a son at all! The pundits have thus advised:
Ajáto-mrto-múrkháńáḿ baramádao na cántimah,
Sakrta duhkhakarávádyávantimastu pade pade.ʼ"
The neighbours asked, “What does the couplet mean?”

The mother explained, “A woman who does not have a son has just one regret. She goes around lamenting that she is childless. A woman whose son has died also has just one regret. She beats her head in sorrow and cries, 'Oh, my son is gone forever, no one will call me má anymore!ʼ But a mother whose son is a fool is doomed forever. On the one hand, she is in misery all the time and on the other, her neighbours call upon her day in and day out to complain about the foolish deeds committed by the son. Listening and listening to all these noises day in and day out I am extremely vexed; my heart is keen to flee. Hence learned men have said, it is better not to have a son at all or even lose a son to death, rather than be saddled with a fool of a son all your life. If such is the case, a mother has to endure agony every moment. You can very well see the plight I am in with this fool Dantavikásh [literal meaning is to display oneʼs teeth foolishly]. Even the fox in the wild and mosquitoes in watery bogs cry in sympathy. Just see with your own eyes how cruelly he beat me on my back. It is swollen like a guŕ-pit́he.”
“That is it!” cried Dantavikásh with joy. “That is it! That is it! Why did you not tell me earlier?”
The teacher asked Bhulo, “You were seen with mangoes in your pockets. Tell me honestly, did you steal them from the Boseʼs orchard?”

Bhulo stuttered, “No, sir . . . I did not sir . . . steal mangoes, sir. Not at all. I was . . . just passing under the mango trees . . . it was Jhulo, sir . . . throwing stones he was . . . at the mangoes hanging from the trees. I was afraid, sir . . . falling mangoes would hurt my head . . .so I ran away, sir. But those mangoes were faster than me, sir. Some of them . . . caught up with me and – and entered my pockets, sir. I did not steal . . . it was Jhulo, sir. If he had not thrown stones . . . the mangoes would still be in the trees, sir . . . and not in my pockets. Once you advised us, sir, not to hold on to stolen things. So I did not keep the mangoes . . . I ate them with salt and chillies.”
The teacher asked Bhoṋdá, “Why do your fingers smell of biŕi [a kind of cigarette rolled from a leaf]?”

Bhoṋdá stuttered, “You know, sir . . . I never. . . such things I never smoke . . . in fact, I do not even utter the name, sir . . . actually it was Khyáṋdá . . . he asked me to hold the thing, sir . . . while he dragged on it. Once you taught us to be good to our friends, did you not, sir? That is why I did not want to hurt Khyáṋdá, sir . . . so my fingers stink. After smoking that thing Khyáṋdá told me . . . let me suck on a lozenge so that my mouth does not smell . . . I asked him to rub the lozenge on my fingers but Khyáṋdá refused . . . he said my fingers will become sticky in that case . . . he had the full lozenge himself. That is why, sir, his mouth smells fresh now while my fingers stink. I never, sir . . . I never smoke such things, sir.”
Varńa Vicitrá Part 4

When one buys a new dress, a house, a car or cooks a new dish, one expects that others will come and give praise because of the word korá [literal meaning, “brand new”] which means “to encourage sound”. When one wears a new dress, the neighbour is supposed to ask, “When did you buy it? How much did it cost?” When you build a new house; you secretly wish that your friends will come and shower compliments. When you buy a new car, you would like your friends to ask, “Which model is it?” When a new dish is prepared, you expect to hear, “Where did you learn to cook so well?”

While discussing this curiosity to know about something new or the eagerness to be questioned, I remember the historically renowned incident which happened at the famous Kháro village. Kháro is a large village well-known for its educated inhabitants although some naughty people said that the intellectual standard of the inhabitants did not grow with their learning.

The day the 500 student of the village acquired a Masterʼs degree, the elders unanimously decided to celebrate the event in a big way. The lát́sáhib from Patna would be invited. (This was during the British days. Rájya [state] or the title Rájyapál [the governor of a state] had not come into use at that time. A provincial Governor or chot́o lát́báhádur was the prevalent term.)

The thought was quickly translated into action. Festivities started in Kháro in no time. The lát́sáhib graced the Presidentʼs chair with a sweet smile. As is normally the custom when invited to speak on such occasions, he praised the excellence of the long tradition and erudition of the Kháro people in glowing terms. He further added that he did indeed hear a few random, uncomplimentary remarks about the village folks, but never believed such nonsense, for today he himself was a witness to their cultural pre-eminence. He could very well perceive that their intellectual level was of the highest order. He promised to issue a press release as soon as he returned to the city in order to dispel all doubts.

The lát́sáhib boarded his car for the return journey. Hordes of educated young men gathered around him. The young man who had been given the responsibility of escorting him back was an M.A. (tryahasparsha) ( 1 ). His two other companions were also very worthy scholars, rivalling each other in intelligence.
The bright red-coloured agricultural fields on both sides of the car, stretched to the horizon.
The lát́sáhib was curious, “What is that red-coloured crop?”
“Morcái, morcái,” cried the lads in excitement (morcái are red chillies, mirc in Hindi).
The lát́sáhib said, “Excellent! It looks so beautiful!”

The young men asked the driver to stop the car for a while. They got down, ran to the fields and collected chillies to fill a sack. They put the sack by the seat of the honoured guest and said, “The chillies cultivated by our people are world famous. These are sent to all parts of India and even exported abroad. You have blessed our village as well as the chillies by kindly consenting to come here. The capital city is a long way off. You might feel bored on the way. Please keep these red chillies for company and munch on them when you feel like it. It will get rid of your boredom and fatigue.”
The lát́sáhibʼs eyes widened and he stared at them in disbelief.
This is, then, the historically famous village of Kháro. Let me tell you what happened when a new object was purchased by a villager named Bhutnarayan Singh.

He was a young, prosperous farmer, well-educated and of good taste. He had a discussion with his friend Bhutnandan Singh. Their village was highly developed but no one had a single watch. It was not befitting the glorious status of Kháro, they decided. A watch was absolutely essential.
In no time, Bhutnarayan disposed of a small portion of his land and went to Kolkata with Rs 5,000. He went to a watchmaker and said, “Take this money. I want the best watch that you have.”

The shopkeeper sized up this customerʼs nature easily. He picked up the smallest and most expensive watch and handed it over. Why should Bhutnarayan be satisfied with a small watch? He saw bigger watches all around.
He said, “Why should I buy a small watch for Rs. 5000? I want the largest.”

The shopkeeper selected a large watch, which was also the cheapest, and told his customer, “This is a dual purpose watch. It will give you the time and additionally, you can throw it to bring down mangoes from the trees.”
Bhutnarayan was very happy.

He returned to his village. He strapped the watch on his wrist all through the day and night and loitered about the locality. He rolled up his sleeve every time he came upon a group of people. But, unfortunately, no one asked him, “When did you buy the watch?”

Then, one morning before the break of dawn, Bhutnarayan set fire to his own house. At the sight of the fire, neighbours from far and near came running to put it out. A crowd gathered all round the house and, since there was no fire brigade in the area, everyone ran helter-skelter with buckets of water to quench the fire. There was a big commotion.

Bhutnarayan moved around the assemblage showing off his watch and remarked, “The fire started at exactly 55 minutes past 5. This watch gives you the time. It can also be thrown to bring down mangoes.”

But no one paid any heed to him. Bhutnarayan repeated his act to many but could not elicit a reaction. The fire was on the point of being extinguished! As a last desperate effort, Bhutnarayan ran to a small gathering and shouted at the top of his voice, “I already told you the fire started at exactly 5:55. It is remarkable how accurately this watch works! It serves another purpose too. You can throw it to bring down mangoes.”
Finally, someone in the crowd remarked, “When did you buy the watch?” Someone else asked, “Where did you buy it?” “How much did it cost?” asked another. “Oh, it is beautiful!” cried someone else.
Bhutnarayan Singh struck his head with his palm and lamented, “If you had reacted like this, if you had uttered these words before, then why would a fool set his own house on fire?”
This, then, is the historically famous village of Kháro.

t: There lived a glutton named Pot́ol Ghosh in my village. When invited to a feast, his minimum intake of luci was 101 pieces. (Luci or nuci are both correct) [luci is a thin, round bread fried in ghee or oil.]

Just as he crossed fifty years of age, he began to suffer from terrible acidity in his stomach. He carried a container of sodium bicarbonate all the time. However, he never ate fewer than 101 luci in a feast to keep his championʼs status intact.
I used to ask him, “Why 101? One hundred is a nice, round number!”
He replied, “I eat the hundredth luci and then, to warn in advance that I am able to eat a thousand in future, I take the extra one.”
Announcing in advance is known as “prior intimation”.

Shráddhe ca bhuribhojanam was a custom in the past. This meant that the invitees to a shráddha [a feast held after funeral rites are performed] were to be treated in a grand fashion. In its common usage, the meaning of the word bhuri is “plenty”, and in this context the quantity of luci, sweets, etc. that was packed inside the guestʼs stomach was to be served on an adjacent plate in an equal amount. After the meal was over, the other plateful of food was tied up in a bundle (cháṋdá) and taken home by the guest. Even after a surfeit of food (such a huge meal had been taken that the food had risen past the abdomen and chest and reached the throat), it was only when the guest carried an equal amount home that it was accepted that it had indeed been a grand feast (bhuribhojana).

In those days, during a feast, when one mumbled to the person serving food, “Huṋ-Huṋ-Huṋ-Huṋ-Huṋ, what are you up to?... no more for me, no more... rather, serve ten sweets to this gentleman.” What he really meant was, “give ten sweets to me and ten more to bring home”. It was the custom to serve the guest even if he apparently declined to eat.

Another guest would speak, while eating, “Hṋá-hṋá-hṋá, what are you up to? Is it possible for me to eat another twenty sweets! Poor me, suffering from diabetes, dyspepsia and chronic dysentery! Do I have the strength to eat twenty more sweets? Well, if you insist, you can serve me twenty-five if you must for now.”

So, it was the custom in those days to serve these gluttons aggressively while they meekly protested and tried to ward off food in a tentative manner. If anyone would say, waving their palms while covering their dish, “What are you doing! Please serve me no more. Can I eat fifteen sweets? But if you are really willing, give me thirty for the time being. I will decide later if I can take more afterwards.” Such a person must be served with more sweets. If someone, shaking the head while expressing their unwillingness, declares, “Give me no more. Once I used to eat 20 kśiirmohan [a particular kind of delicious sweet made of milk] in one swallow voraciously. Nowadays I canʼt. Those days I would eat twenty sweets in one swallow. Nowadays, even twenty-five tire me out. You want to give me ten oh no, I canʼt eat that much. But you can give twenty-five on a trial basis.” In this case, you must serve them twenty-five sweets. You will cease only when someone leaps up like a tiger, presses your hands together and implores, “Give me no more! I canʼt eat any more!”
It has been said for the guidance of those who served in a feast that,
Huṋ-huṋ deyaḿ hṋá-hṋá deyam,
Deyaḿ ca karakampane,
Shirasi cálane deyam,
Na deyaḿ vyághrajhampane.
[Serve those who say Huṋ-huṋ and hṋá-h̭á,
Serve those who decline by waving palms,
Serve those who shake their heads,
Desist only when one leaps up like a tiger.]
I have narrated to you the picture of a glutton of olden days. Oaodarika (using the inflection ook) or pet́uka in Bengal and pet́u in northern India means a voracious eater.

Kut́t́anii or kut́anii is one who is not straightforward, one who takes a devious approach all the time. Kaot́t́anii or kaot́t́anika is the word used to describe the nature of kut́t́anii. Kut́t́anii + ań = kaot́t́anii, and kut́t́anii + t́hak = kaot́t́anika. The vidyá [knowledge or cunning and manipulative skill] is known as kut́t́anii vidyá or kaot́t́anii vidyá. Those who are glum by nature and never smile, like the saying Rám gaŕurer cháná háṋste táder máná ["The young ones of Garud́a, the prince of birds and the carrier of Lord Viśńu, who can never smile"] – are called kut́t́aniimukha in colloquial Bengali.

This reminds me of an old incident. I knew a railway officer by the name of, say, Gobar Ganesh Gayen. He put on a sour face all the time. When I asked him in private, “Why do you keep up such an unpleasant visage?” He replied, “My subordinates will take me for granted if I smiled.”
I said, “Even if you do not laugh with them, what is the harm in talking to people?”
He said, “That will make me look cheap.”
I said, “Is this the reason why you want to keep people at a distance and remain fine (khástá)?”
“Yes,” he said, without a smile.

Once, a grand picnic was organized. There was going to be a lavish feast with poláo, káliá, etc., and huge brinjals from the winter season, as big as bottle-gourds, brought all the way from Kashi. When the food was cooked and ready, about fifty to sixty big brinjals were left over. It was decided to roast the brinjals and serve them for a change of taste.

Wasting no time, the roasted brinjals were served first when we sat down to eat. [[Gobar Ganesh Gayen let his guard down when he said, in order to encourage everyone,]] “These are delicious, absolutely first class!”
Someone quipped, “No, not first class, even better; these are air-conditioned class.”
[[Gobar Ganesh spoke again in a somewhat serious tone, saying “Anyhow, they’re very tasty.”]]

Samar Sengupta, whom I knew well, did not lose the opportunity. He immediately quipped, “Sir, if roasted brinjals taste good, I am sure the other items will also go down well with the roasted face, ( 1 ) you will see.”
[[Gobar Ganesh did not catch the jibe, and in an even more serious manner fixed his attention on eating.]]
No one likes people of this nature. When they keep slighting everyone, people retaliate as soon as an opportunity arises.
You should never indulge in such behaviour. It is good [[neither]] for society nor for yourself.
Varńa Vicitrá Part 4

It was the practice in ancient times to predict the fate of the State and of individuals by studying the zodiac position at the time of birth, but subsequently karakośt́hii or Palmistry (palmistry did not originate in ancient India. The Brahmans in Shákadviipa [Southern region of Russia – what is today Uzbekistan, Kazakistan and Tajikistan] had imported the knowledge from the other side of the ocean; hence, it is named sámudrik vidyá [maritime knowledge]) was invented and popularized.

Based on an individualʼs name and specific number related to his or her past reactive momenta (saḿskára), the art of telling oneʼs fate developed at a later time. The art of crystal gazing and nail gazing gained popularity about three thousand years ago. All these skills were practised by astrologers and palmists.

It must be mentioned that the various skills of astrology were not absolute and free from errors. However, some people would argue that a prediction was likely to be erroneous if it was based on wrong data or calculations. Hence, it would be unfair to blame the very art of astrology.

Though their arguments cannot be discounted summarily, no one should be totally dependent on astrological predictions. People should boldly move onwards, according to their own efforts (puruśakára) and abilities.
Daevaḿ nihatya kuru paoruśamátmashaktyá.
[Never depend on fate but on own courage and effort.]

Even when astrological calculations are done skilfully, The Horoscope of Ramphal Singh 135 it is not necessary that predictions will turn out to be true in all cases. If the son of a king and the son of a common man are born under the same zodiac sign, then, it is quite possible that on that one evening when the prince was being crowned as the king, the commoner would be acting in the role of a king in a village play. He would then be addressed by the other actors as the king.

There was a newborn baby who was named Ramphal Singh. An astrologer made calculations on his planetary position (dashá, antardashá) [primary and secondary planetary influence on human life] at the time of birth and predicted that he would live a life of affluence with cars all around him. He was indeed very fortunate, exclaimed the astrologer.

Therefore, the near and dear ones of the baby and friends kept waiting for the day when Ramphal Singhʼs destiny would be revealed in full splendour. Twenty-four years went by. Ramphal Singh had finally became a traffic constable, standing on the crossroads with cars rushing around him.
Whatever it may be, I do not think the astrologers are always wrong. I have myself seen some of their predictions come true. But you should never rely entirely on them.

Once, two factions of the followers of the Prophet Mohammed had a heated altercation between themselves. One side said that destiny (takdir) was all powerful, while the other group said that it was perseverance and hard work (tadvir) which shaped a manʼs future. The wrangling devotees approached the Prophet.
He listened to both groups and said, “You have to go on working hard (tadvir) although destiny (takdir) will prevail.”

chapterTitle: The Brahmanʼs Son Who Was A Fool

t: [One who accompanies you to the gate of the Royal Palace as well as to the cremation ground after your death is a true friend.]
chapterTitle: The Brahmanʼs Son Who Was A Fool

t: He could see a cremation ground near the donkey. Since the creature was at such a place, he concluded it must be a friend. He went to the donkey, embraced him round the neck and said affectionately, “My friend, find me a place to spend the night.”
chapterTitle: The Brahmanʼs Son Who Was A Fool

t: The donkey began to bray and jump around in dismay. That brought the donkeyʼs master, a washerman, running there with a stick in his hand. He beat the stupid pundit thoroughly. The fool escaped with his life and ran at lightning speed like a jackal with its tail tucked between its legs.
chapterTitle: The Brahmanʼs Son Who Was A Fool
The Brahmanʼs Son Who Was A Fool

t: These two stupid men had another companion. This man had found shelter for the night in a house. His host offered him vermicelli porridge (semái páyes). The punditʼs son had never seen such food in his life as he had been brought up on cheap rice and boiled plantains since his childhood.
chapterTitle: The Brahmanʼs Son Who Was A Fool

t: He promptly took out his holy books to learn about this food. Vermicelli looks like a slender thread, which is sútriká in Sanskrit. He did not know this. However, he came across a clue – diirghasútrii vinashyati. Actually, diirghasútrii means psychology of procrastination (to dawdle, to postpone).
chapterTitle: The Brahmanʼs Son Who Was A Fool

t: Hence, the adage means that people who procrastinate are heading for destruction. The stupid pundit thought that since vermicelli was long and threadlike, it must be diirghasútrii and he would inevitably die if he ate the food. The host was trying to kill him, he thought. So he fled swiftly from the place.
chapterTitle: The Brahmanʼs Son Who Was A Fool
The Brahmanʼs Son Who Was A Fool

t: These three friends had a fourth companion who was also wondering where to put up for the night. A man passed by. He came to know that this man was a moneylender (mahájana) who lived on interest. In Sanskrit, mahájana is a word which is used to mean different things such as a great man, a moneylender, a rich man or a wholesaler.
chapterTitle: The Brahmanʼs Son Who Was A Fool

t: The stupid pundit consulted his erudite books and came upon an adage – mahájano yena gatah sah panthá – which means, “The path taken by a great man is the right path and the rest should follow in his footsteps.”
chapterTitle: The Brahmanʼs Son Who Was A Fool

t: So he followed the usurer. The moneylender looked back from time to time and found that a stranger was following him. He took him to be a robber. The man caught hold of the stupid pundit and beat him black and blue. The stupid pundit mused, “To flee is the only true lesson in life.” He forgot all his scriptures and ran away with great agility shouting, “Am I so scared that my feet are frozen? No, never!”

t: The use of cha is prevalent in the native dialects of Bengal but it is pronounced differently in various dialects. The cha sound in a foreign word is pronounced as cha or ca or even as sa in the Bengali dialects of different regions. Many use the letter cha to represent the sa sound in Arabic words. Although it does not correctly represent the Arabic sa sound, there is nothing wrong with it because it tries to emulate a distinctive pronunciation at least. Therefore, there is no problem in using both forms of spellings for words like Syed and Chyed, Islam and Echlam, Basiruddin and Bachiruddin.
Sushil Majumdar, a friend of mine, was very much opposed to such use of cha. He had even written a story ridiculing the practice. A portion of it reads as follows:
Chuchilbábur cehárár chahit Bánglár
chubedárer cehárár chádrichya áche.
Chutaráḿ Chuchilbábu je ekkále Bánglár
chipáhchálár chilen táháte chandeha nái.
[Sushil bábu has facial similarities to the subádár (governor of a province in Moghul India) of Bengal. Hence, there is no doubt that he was once the commander of Bengal.]

However, I do not agree with Sushil. I am in favour of The Story of Sushil Majumdar 143 using cha when necessary. One has to admit that cha does signify a special sound and it should be used where needed. But such use of cha should only be limited to Arabic words and should not be permitted to pollute Persian words. Like Pushtu, Persian is a refined generic, sanskritic language; it is Semitic in origin like Arabic or Hebrew. These two languages [Arabic and Persian] are as different from each other as the sky and the earth. Persian was not written in the evolved Arabian script during the time of Zarathurashtra or even much later during the rule of Darius. It used [a form of] the Bráhmii-kharośt́hii script.

The verbal root jan in Sanskrit became jand in old Persian, from which was derived the words jádá and jádii. The son of Bádsháh (emperor) is known as Bádsháhjádá, the daughter, Bádsháhjádii. A kingʼs son is called Sháhjádá, daughter, Sháhjádii. In this connection, you may have heard of a story.

Once, a mother-in-law and her daughter-in-law quarrelled after the former rained cruel abuses on the latter. Suddenly during the quarrel, the mother-in-lawʼs jaws became locked. She was unable to speak.

Well-known doctors from every field of the medical profession were called in but to no avail. Finally, a veterinary doctor came who did something to her cheeks. The womanʼs jaws were set right and the word jádii sprang out.
Actually, her jaws had become locked when she called her daughter-in-law hárám [dirty, inedible swine] and now, she completed the abuse with jádii [daughter of dirty swine].
Once, I was passing through a village in Hooghly district when I witnessed comradeship in a fight between the husband and wife of a household.

The wife lamented bitterly, “Oh, how unfortunate I am to come to this family! I am fed up to the marrow... oh dear, dear, please have some more porridge. Just for you, I used raisins in the recipe, but you are not having enough! If you do not eat more, then for which accursed rascal did I cook it for? What a mean family this is! Why am I stuck here for life and getting tortured? Please take a second helping, dear. You had better skip afternoon snacks. I cannot cook this delicacy every day, can I? I made this porridge with flattened rice, next time I shall make it with bottle-gourd. Oh, I hate this family, being here is a punishment for my sins in past lives! Die, die, die! Oh, my dear, do not swallow so fast, what if you choke? Here, take a sip from this glass of water from time to time. Do not drink so much that your stomach gets full and you are unable to eat more. This is irritating, this is too irritating. He is irritating me even when eating food!... I shall leave for my fatherʼs house at once!”
The husband said in a low voice, “If you leave, what shall I have for dinner tonight?”

The wife said, “Dinner will be cooked and kept ready. No accursed rascal should worry about that, only adept at gorging down food, he is!” The husband said rather warily, “Tonight is taken care of, but what shall I eat tomorrow?”
“No accursed rascal need worry about that too! I shall come here tomorrow and prepare the food. Let the rascal devour it!”
The husband said, still more warily, “This is Dashghara village and your fatherʼs house is in Dwarbasini. Is it possible to come from such a long distance everyday to cook?”

The woman was aghast, “What audacity! Telling me about what is possible and what is impossible? What good are you? You have to take up tuition classes on top of your teaching job in school to earn enough to run this family when you are an M.A. in three subjects! Die, die, die! What good is the teacher who gave you those certificates? I wish I could have a go at that scoundrel! In any case, you do not have to worry about food, your only job will be to gulp it down.”

Well, this is the story. Both the warring partners were sincere in their minds. But the womanʼs energy was so overwhelming that even an elephant – let alone the meek husband – would have been swept away like khaŕkut́o ( 1 ) [dry straw and twigs].
Now you know what comradeship in a fight is (doshtii mein kustii).
The meaning of the verbal root jap is to mutter repeatedly. When the inflection d́a is added to the root jap, the letter ja [jap] is formed, which has two meanings.
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: One meaning, of course, is the man who is praying silently with his beads, and the other is the Supreme Being to whom the prayer is dedicated. One who says the same thing over and over again is said to be japácche [persistent]. There is no synonym for japa in English.
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: There are three kinds of japa. The first is oral japa, when the prayer is audible (vácanika). In upáḿshu japa, the lips move though no sound is uttered. The third is mánasika [mental] japa, when the mind prays and listens. It is said that mental japa is the highest form, followed by upáḿshu japa and, finally, oral japa. In oral prayer, oneʼs mind may wander into extraneous thoughts.
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: It may also be remembered that while doing japa, first, one must understand the meaning of the words used, and second, the idea behind the japa must always be pictured in the mind.
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: In this context, I am reminded of a second aunt of the Chatterjee family in Naihati. She took initiation at a much advanced age.
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: Her guru (master) had told her, “Repeating Harekrśńa Harekrśńa over and over is your japa.” She was in a quandary. Hari was her husbandʼs name, Krśńa was the name of her husbandʼs elder brother. In those days, a woman never uttered the names of her elders as a mark of respect.
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: The aunt slyly changed her prayer to “e báŕiir uni, o báŕiir baŕat́hákur” [my husband here, his elder brother there].
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: Needless to say, such cleverness belies the very idea of prayer. It is as futile as chanting phay phagannáth phathe ut́heche, pharibol, pharibol, because the words Joy, Jagannath, Rath, and Hari, etc. were the names of the womanʼs husband, father-in-law, brother-in-law and uncle-in-law respectively. This is no prayer at all according to the scriptures. Chanting a prayer in such a manner does not benefit any one. It is written in Tantra:
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: Caetanyarahitáh mantráh proktovarńáhastu kevalám,
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: Phalaḿ naeva prayacchanti lakśakot́i japaerapi.
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: [Mantras without their corresponding ideation are merely a couple of letters mechanically uttered. They will not bear any fruit even if repeated a billion times.]
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: My grandmother met the woman who chanted phay phagannáth in Puri. She addressed my grandma as Brahmanpara and my grandma called her Haripál, which were actually places from where they originally came.
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: Once my grandma asked her, “You do not utter the word Hari, then how do you tell people where you come from?” Immediately she replied, “Why, I say Pharipál!”
chapterTitle: Never Take the Name of Hari!

t: In Bengali, the word nolá [greedy for food] is derived from lol(*) or loltá. For example, garmágaram singárá, ekebáre kholá theke nolá, that is, hot singárá [a delicious stuffed snack] goes straight from the frying pan into the mouth. This reminds me of an incident.

In her in-lawʼs house, a woman was made to toil hard all day. No one even cared to find out if she had enough food to eat. One day, she felt greedy at the sight of the thick layer of cream on the pot of milk. But her in-laws were nearby; hence, it was impossible to put her lips to the pot without being seen. She resisted the urge and said to herself:
O nolá,
Tapta kholá
Sámle cal, sámle cal,
Yave yábi báper ghar,
Tule khábi dudher sar,
Ekhan ki ár karbi bal.
[O my audacious greed!
The pot is very hot,
So get a hold of yourself.
When you go to your fatherʼs house,
You may have as many layers of milk as you wish.
But for now there is nothing to do.]

In rural Bengal there is a saying, “A woman is very greedy”, but is it right to say so? Both men and women are greedy, and honestly, a woman is less greedy than a man. Do you understand now what is nolá?

Those who are excessively greedy are known as noladár or noládágá in colloquial Bengali. I knew such a gentleman very well. When invited to a feast, no fewer than one hundred nuchi [luci – thin bread fried in ghee] would be sufficient for him. He knew he might fall sick, and hence he always carried with him a tin of sodium bicarbonate. Even the thought of falling ill could not deter him from eating more than what was good for him. Just think of his voracious greed! It was like this:
Shariirtá áj bejáy kháráp, bisheś kichui khábo ná,
Ser páṋcek máḿsa dio, chap-cutlet́ du-cár kháná.
Rosogollá hálká jinis, bish serkeo karbo finish,
Sandesh ektu bhárii boley áshir beshii párbo ná.
Báro bháṋŕer beshii doi pratham dapháy dio ná,
Shariirtá áj bejáe kháráp bisheś kichui khábo ná.

[I am not well today, I shall not have much to eat, Serve me just about five seers of meat, a few fries and cutlets, Sweetmeats are light, so finishing twenty seers will not be a problem. However, sandesh is a sweetmeat made from milk, Which is rather difficult to digest, therefore eighty of them will be all right. Do not serve more than a dozen earthen pots of sweet curd in the first helping, You see, I am not well today, I shall not have much to eat.]

Are you surprised to find “finish”, an English word, used in a Bengali rhyme? No, you should not be. A unanimous decision was once taken at a joint meeting of “rockfellars” (a group of young men who idled their time away chatting while seated on the raised terrace in the front part of a house) and “parkers” (those who chatted in parks for hours) in Kolkata that the best piece of poetry ever written by Rabindranath Tagore was:
Enechile sáthe kore mrityuhin jinis,
Morańe táhái tumi kare gele finish.
[You had brought with you a deathless spirit, Which was extinguished by your own death.]
Excessive eating is a disease of the mind. Everyone should try to desist from it. Shiva said,
Atibhojanaḿ rogamúlamáyuhkśayakaram,
Tasmádatibhojanaḿ sarvathá pariharet.
[Voracious eating is the cause of all disease. It reduces oneʼs lifespan. You must avoid overeating at all cost.]
In Bengali, it is said, unobháte duno bal bhará pet́e rasátal [eat less and gain more strength, overeating is the way to ruin].
Káli tor kál koreche lolrasaná
dekhe muńd́amálá háte kháṋŕá
japate torey man sare na.
[Oh Kali, your greed has been your drawback your garland of scalps and the scimitar in your hand frighten me from chanting your name.]

Of all types of hypocritical behaviour, we are more familiar with three very common patterns. The first is to exploit others or deceive them in order to fulfill oneʼs own interests. The second is to browbeat others to hide oneʼs own ignorance or fault, and the third is to castigate an offence publicly with a view to proving oneʼs innocence, when in fact one is actually a party to the crime.
chapterTitle: Mr Nag in a Crowded Train

t: I shall narrate an incident to exemplify the first kind of hypocrisy. I knew a gentleman in Tamluk who held a high position in office. Let us say his name was Mr Nag.
chapterTitle: Mr Nag in a Crowded Train

t: Once he was travelling from Kolkata to Darjeeling during the [Durgá] Pújá vacation. It was during the British days.
chapterTitle: Mr Nag in a Crowded Train

t: The train was very crowded. It was quite obvious from a look at his fellow passengers that they were not going to disembark at Ranaghat or Porada or even Santahar. Mr Nag remained standing. After some time, he suddenly spoke, “Now I understand why Gandhijii advised me never to travel in a crowded compartment. We are small people and so I thought that he was probably worried about my own comfort. But the thought never crossed his mind. Gandhijii is a great man, much more superior to ordinary people like us. He then explained, “I am telling you all of this not for your own convenience. I am feeling sorry about the discomfort of your fellow passengers because as soon as you enter the crowded compartment, the head count goes up by one, causing more inconvenience to them!” I am always overwhelmed with deep respect for the man [Gandhijii] when I think of his wonderful words. I consider myself exceptionally fortunate for having had the opportunity to serve him. I feel honoured, honoured.”
chapterTitle: Mr Nag in a Crowded Train

t: The fellow passengers exclaimed, “Is that so, sir? You were Gandhijiʼs companion?” It was the last days of the British Raj. Gandhiji was a great influence on Indian society and he was held in high esteem. Everyone clamoured, “Sir, tell us about Gandhiji.”
chapterTitle: Mr Nag in a Crowded Train

t: Mr Nag said, “All right. I spent a month in his company. I looked after him. I served him food in his room. I milked his goat and massaged his body with walnut oil.”
chapterTitle: Mr Nag in a Crowded Train

t: “Please continue sir, please tell us all about Gandhiji.”
chapterTitle: Mr Nag in a Crowded Train

t: Mr Nag said, “In that case, let me sit comfortably.”
chapterTitle: Mr Nag in a Crowded Train

t: Everyone shouted, “Give him a seat, give the respected sir a seat.”
chapterTitle: Mr Nag in a Crowded Train

t: A seat was provided to Mr Nag.
