t: We come across the second kind of hypocrisy very often also. I remember an incident. A man afflicted with rheumatism once went to see a quack doctor. The doctor listened to his patientʼs complaint and asked, “Do you feel pain in your stomach?” The patient replied, “No. There is no pain in my stomach.”
The quack said in a bullying voice, “Of course there is pain, but you are not aware of it (ay, ay, zánti páraná).” After a pause he asked, “Is there an ache in your gums?”
“No, sir, there is no ache in my gums.”
The doctor gave him a massive rebuke, “Of course there is, but you are not aware of it. Do you suffer from malaria in your big toe?”
The patient meekly said, “No sir, I never had malaria in my big toe nor, for that matter, in any of my other toes.”
The quack thundered, “Of course you have, you are simply not aware of it. Is there typhoid in the root of your ear?”
“No sir, I do not have typhoid in the root or in any other parts of the ear.”
The quack chastised him heavily, “Of course you have, but you are simply not aware of it.”
The patient said softly, “In that case sir, when I am cured of this byámo ( 1 ) [disease], I might not be aware if I am cured or not.”

The third kind of hypocrisy is also very common. I heard that a man in America had once started a strong protest movement against the evils of alcoholism. He spoke strongly about the ill effects of drinking to a gathering for a full hour. Then he said, “My throat is dry, give me a glass of brandy.”

I was travelling from Sahibgunj to Dumka by car It was a long journey. As I left the city of Sahibgunj behind, I came upon beautiful scenery of hills and forests. The scenic beauty of the remote regions of western Ráŕh was simply awesome. I had a desire to take a walk amidst the splendour. I stepped down from the car and started to walk.

After I had walked a little distance, I came across a small boy of seven or eight who did not have any clothes on but who wore a pair of new shoes. He was poking inside a hole in the ground with a slip of bamboo.
I asked him in the local dialect, “What is your name?”
“Ramkrishna Turii,” said he.
“What are you up to?”
“Catching rats.”
“What will you do with a rat?”
“Roast it and eat it.”
I asked, “Does everyone here eat rats?”
“Yes, everyone.”
“Even the upper castes – Brahmans and Kayasthas?”
He said, “Yes, but they eat it in secret.”
This manner of eating some forbidden thing on the sly is an attempt to hide oneʼs own guilt. It is also hypocritical.

In indigenous words, the pronunciation t́a is properly retained and d́a and ŕa remain as primary words. For example, ‘Bhulo and Bhoṋdá terminated (áŕi) their friendship today. They decided not to play marbles together anymore and not to share the same guava.’ Also, áŕi pátá means to eavesdrop on someone. This is also an indigenous usage in spoken Bengali.
A lady who was beside herself with joy once told a friend, “I cannot express in words how glad I feel on seeing you.”
Her friend said, “Just give me a hint of how happy you feel.”
The lady replied, “I am so happy that the whole world seems like a small saucer to me.”

As it happened, a farmer had lost his cow and had been searching all day to find it. Tired to his bones, he was resting on the veranda of a house at that time when he overheard the ladies talking inside. He began to dance joyously and pleaded to the lady, “If the world really appears to be a small saucer to you, please do tell me at which spot in the saucer I shall find my cow.”

According to many people, a debate is related to logic or an argumentative act. The interpretation is partially correct since a particular kind of war of words is called a “debate”. However, that is not all. Intolerable chattering is also classified as debate. When peevishness or bragging is mixed with ill temper and incessant talking, it is considered more a debate than bitter argument (kaśay) [kaśáy means bitter or astringent taste].
I shall narrate a few incidents of debates of various kinds.
A man reached Howrah station. He was a bit late. He asked a gentleman, “Has the local train to Uluberia left?”

The gentleman said irritably, “Is it my job to keep track of Uluberia locals? Am I a timetable? Such silly people all around... decidedly stupid... this is why this country is in such a mess... he thinks I am the Enquiry office! Ha!”
There was a man standing nearby. He said, “Are you enquiring about the Uluberia local? It is delayed by five minutes and will depart from platform no. 11. You can catch it if you hurry.”
The first instance is an example of debate, the second is of reticence (pramitaváka). A reticent man is economical in speech; he never says more than what is necessary.

It was a family of just father and son. The father went to the market while the son cooked food for his father to eat. The father sat down to eat and exclaimed in the local dialect, “Oooh, Ramchandra! How many chillies did you put in the curry?”
“Six gańd́á ( 1 )”, said the son.
“How many did I tell you to put?”
“Thirty-two, father (eight gańd́á).”
“And you have put how many?”
“Twenty-four.”
“I will not eat this food, I will not!” cried the father.
“Please forgive me for the last time. I promise I shall not make the mistake again.”

“The Ramchandra of ancient times went into self-exile for fourteen years just to honour his fatherʼs words. And you! Ramchandra of today! You are violating your fatherʼs command! Tell me, how many chillies did I tell you to put?”
“Eight gańd́á, father.”
“And how many did you put?”
“Six gańd́á, father.”
“You have violated your fatherʼs command. I will not eat this food. I will kick away the plate and break it.”

It was a big museum. A man who had the habit of talking incessantly had been appointed the curator. Talking was what he lived for. He kept his job and hoped to get promotions though intolerable chattering.

He used to exhibit a small skull to the visitors of the museum and explain, “You will all be surprised to know that this skull is that of the celebrated King Pratap of historical fame. Of course you do have valid reasons to feel surprised!”
There happened to be a gentleman among the group who was a Professor of History. He spoke up, “But King Pratap was a huge, sturdy man. Why should his skull be so small?”

The curator said, “Truly spoken like a learned man, but you must remember that when King Pratap was young, his skull was small. This skull belongs to his early childhood. When he grew up his skull became large, just as you have pointed out. We do not have that larger skull here in the museum. However, we are not sitting idle sir, we are trying very hard to get hold of it. I can tell you with confidence, sir, that next time you visit us, we shall have it in our possession.”

In my childhood days, there was a female cook in my uncleʼs house at Shyambazar. She was an expert cook like Saerindhrii ( 1 ). We used to call her Bámun didi. Her inherent sense of adding ingredients, such as salt, chili and spices was excellent.
chapterTitle: The Troubles of a Brahman Female Cook

t: A few guests had once been invited to the house. After dinner was over, they showered compliments on Bámun didiʼs marvelous cooking. They said over and over, “Oh, that was delicious! We doubt if she has a parallel anywhere.”
chapterTitle: The Troubles of a Brahman Female Cook

t: Bámun didi was beside herself with joy from so much praise and said, “If I do not cook well, who else will?”
chapterTitle: The Troubles of a Brahman Female Cook

t: When the guests left, my aunt scolded her, “It is proper to beat oneʼs own drum.”
chapterTitle: The Troubles of a Brahman Female Cook

t: She looked questioningly at my aunt and said, “Then what should I have done?”
chapterTitle: The Troubles of a Brahman Female Cook

t: “When someone praises you, you should keep your eyes down, smile demurely and continue to wring your hands all the time. But, inwardly in your mind, you may lap up all the compliments joyfully. Do you understand?”
chapterTitle: The Troubles of a Brahman Female Cook

t: Bámun didi said, “Yes, I do.”
chapterTitle: The Troubles of a Brahman Female Cook

t: A few days later, some other guests came for dinner. Again, they were carried away by the cooking prowess of Bámun didi and were voluble in their praises. They gushed, “This is food for the gods, it is fantastic, even the chefs of heaven could not produce such a feast. The taste will linger for a long time and we shall eagerly wait for the next invitation.”
chapterTitle: The Troubles of a Brahman Female Cook

t: Bámun didi had had her lesson earlier. She was seated at that time but jumped up with alacrity. She cast her eyes downwards, smiled demurely and wrung her hands; she was all ears and enjoyed the compliments immensely in her mind. However, she failed in the last hurdle. In order to appear very modest, she prattled on unnecessarily, “Oh, it is nothing much! What did I cook but some hot and spicy rotten cow dung!”
chapterTitle: The Troubles of a Brahman Female Cook

t: The guests all started spitting.
chapterTitle: The Troubles of a Brahman Female Cook

t: T́hát́h means a receptacle; some of you know that Hindu priests place the shálgrám shilá [sacred stone] in a receptacle on Náráyańaʼs seat. This receptacle is also called t́hát́h. Have you heard the story of the sacred stone in a receptacle? Here it is:

A Hindu priest was travelling with his Náráyańaʼs seat to a rich devoteeʼs house a few miles away. When half way there, the priest discovered that he had forgotten to place the sacred stone in its proper receptacle. What to do now? A priest is a shrewd man of the world. A brainwave came to him instantly.
He picked up the dry shell of a snail from the roadside and placed it on the receptacle, thinking that the disciple would not know the difference.

The priest arrived at the destination and sat down to worship. The initial rites were performed. Then it was time to pour water from a small ladle and bathe the sacred stone (shálgrám shilá ( 1 )) while chanting sacred hymns.

Then the inevitable happened. The dry shell of the snail came alive when water was poured on it. It stirred and began to move out of the receptacle – on to Náráyańaʼs seat and down to the floor it moved freely. The priest sat stunned. His devotee exclaimed, “What is happening?”

The priest, as I had mentioned earlier, was a man of the world. His fertile brain hit upon an idea. He said to the disciple, “What great luck you have! Náráyańa himself has come alive in your house. Never before in history has this happened. The whole of mankind has been blessed by this unique miracle, let alone small people like you and me. You should commemorate this historic event by increasing tenfold what you had intended to offer in devotion and in charity to me. It will be a fitting gesture for all of us to remember it by.”

The devotee could plainly see that it was a snail on the move but kept his mouth shut due to reverence and awe. He said meekly, “I had offered one sháŕii [womanʼs clothing] to the goddess. Do I now have to give ten?”
“I do not like repeating,” said the priest.
“Well sir, Kali, the Mother Goddess does not wear any clothes. What will she do with so many sháŕii?”

“Who put these rubbish thoughts in your head?” said the priest. “Of course she does not wear clothes in a cremation ground, but when she goes shopping or to social functions, she wears expensive clothes – either printed silk sháŕii from Murshidabad or Benaras. You may not find such costly sháriis in this locality. However, superior quality sháŕiis and dhotis from Dhanekhali or Shantipur will serve the purpose for now. The Mother will not object, neither shall I.”
The disciple mumbled, “But sir, Shiva moves around nude or, at the most, wrapped in a tiger skin. What will he do with ten dhotis [menʼs apparel]?”

“You tried your best again but to no avail,” said the priest. “The case for Shiva is the same. He might wear a tiger skin in the cremation ground, but do you expect him to come and move around in this locality wearing nothing or just a tiger skin! If he ever comes here, he will be wearing the finest dhoti and frilled páiṋjábii [upper dress] or pants and a bush shirt. However, making pants is troublesome because you need correct measurements and a good tailor. Why go to so much trouble? It is better to offer him a few fine quality dhotis from Pharasdanga or Shantipur. Many hundreds rupee notes are already in your hands by selling potatoes this year. Also, you can get these here by the dozen if you are willing to shell out money. Shiva is very easy to please. He is satisfied with whatever you offer to Him. He will not be unhappy if you give him dhotis made of coarse cloth, but I could not allow that! How can I ask him to wear cheap cloth? I have not lost my senses, have I? The other night, the Mother Goddess came in my dream. She said, 'I know that you work very hard in your profession. You walk miles in the sun and rain to reach the house of your devotees. I know that you were harassed (nástánábud ( 2 ) ) to the extreme on your way to Chandannagore the other day. My heart bled in sorrow for your sake. Tell your devotee to donate to you a cycle of the latest design and a good quality umbrella this time. You are my son. Tell him that I shall be pleased if he gives you a cycle and an umbrella.ʼ She further added, 'Tell your disciple that both are available in the central market in Chandannagore. He does not have to travel all the way to Kolkata to buy, and since he will be going to the central market, let him also buy five seers of sweet (gajá) [a type of sweet made of flour] to be given away as offering. It will look nice.”
The devotee said, “I shall do what you say.”
He kept his word but a little doubt lingered in his mind because he had seen with his own eyes that the snail had begun to move when water was sprinkled on it.
How do you like the story of sweetmeats from the central market?
A daughter of a t́hákur or father-in-law has come to be known as t́hákurjhi in this way:
t́hakkarduhitá > t́hakkurjuhiá > t́hákurjhiá >t́hákurjhi.

A woman calls the sister of her husband t́hákurjhi even now. The husband of that sister (nanad) or nandái (nanandápati > nanandáoi > nandái ) is addressed as t́hákur-jámái, which means the son-in-law of t́hákur [father-in-law]. In some places in Ráŕh, men address the wifeʼs sister as t́hákurjhi as well and, according to philologists, such usage is not incorrect.

Nanandá means one who is not joyous (ánanditá). In fact, some sisters-in-law are known to bear a grudge against their brotherʼs newly married wife. The sister-in-law looks upon the latter as someone who has usurped her rights in her own home, while she herself is nothing but a maidservant in her own in-lawʼs house.

In those days, both the wife and her sister-in-law were not very literate so they continually disagreed on minor matters and could not tolerate each other. Society has turned full circle now. These days, in most families, these two female members are educated and co-exist in peace. It is somewhat like:
Bháve gadagada telákucho,
Keńde mare gelo kálo chuṋco.
[Creeping plants are ecstatic with emotion, And the musk rat died crying.]
In the past, there was bitter rivalry between them. In this connection, I recall an incident:

A woman and her husbandʼs sister went to have a bath in the river. Suddenly, a crocodile surfaced, grabbed the sister-in-law in its jaws and moved away. However, her brotherʼs wife did not tell anyone about it. Inwardly, she was elated for her sister-in-law had always been unkind to her.
Nanadinii ráybághinii, nanadinii kuler káṋt́á,
Ut́hte baste dey go khoṋt́á.
[My sister-in-law is aggressive; she is a thorn in the family, She is spiteful to me all the time.]

So the wife did not tell anyone about the incident when she reached home. She knew that if the bad news spread, there would be a hue and cry. Eating would be out of the question. The cooked food would be thrown outside, delicious items would go to waste as no one would feel like eating. She kept her mouth shut and ate her fill with a quantity of rice so high that even a cat would not be able to jump over it – along with other delicacies, and then stood up by pressing her hands against the floor. She thought grudgingly that she would have to clean up alone.
D́halád́halá puiṋer pátá malukcáler bhát,
Kheye deye rainu bashe ke phelábe pát.
[I ate with relish rice and juicy spinach leaves, But who will clear the leftovers?]
She went to rinse her mouth in the river.

The movement of the animal species belonging to the crocodile genus is rather spasmodic. This is as true for big crocodiles as it is for small wall lizards. Clamping its prey in its jaws, the animal moves away in leaping motions and it appears that the prey is also dancing. The crocodile which had caught her sister-in-law had also moved away in that manner.

Now that lunch was over, the woman decided that it was time to disclose what had happened. No harm even if the rice pot was thrown away, since not a grain was left in it. She had licked it all up. While rinsing her mouth, she announced to everyone:
Bhálo kathá mane paŕlo áṋcáte áṋcáte,
T́hákurjhi ke niye gelo nácáte nácáte.
[Oh, I just remembered while rinsing my mouth, My sister-in-law was taken away dancing by a crocodile.]
Everyone said in surprise, “Why did you not tell us before that your sister-in-law had been a crocodileʼs prey?”
The woman said, “Oh, I just happened to remember it while rinsing my mouth in the river.”

Thakkarputra > t́hakkurputta > t́hakkarpua > t́hákurpo. Etymologically, t́hákurpo means the son of a womanʼs father-in-law. However, t́hákurpo, in common usage, is a form of addressing her deor [husbandʼs younger brother]. The reverse relationship or form of address is bháj or, in modern Bengali, baudi. However, this latter address is a recent coinage and was used more often in modern times.
chapterTitle: The Woman and Her Brother-in-Law of Kaikala

t: Baut́hán was commonly used even up to the middle of British rule. Baout́hákruń was used even earlier, and prior to that baot́hákuráńii and bháj-bou were common forms of address (bhrátrjáyá-badhu > bháij-bahu > bháj-bau).
chapterTitle: The Woman and Her Brother-in-Law of Kaikala

t: There is no literary or historical documentation of the form of bháj before that period for the simple reason that Bengali language did not exist then.
chapterTitle: The Woman and Her Brother-in-Law of Kaikala

t: Bháj-bau was in use in the intermediate stage between half-Prákrta and old Bengali. Have you heard the story of the man and his elder brotherʼs wife, both of whom were deaf?
chapterTitle: The Woman and Her Brother-in-Law of Kaikala

t: Once there was a woman and her brother-in-law. They were both stone deaf. They lived in Kaikala. The brother-in-law sported long hair. Only researchers can say if he aspired to be stylish or wanted to save money by not having a haircut. We cannot comment on that. The woman held a wooden chopping board (boṋt́i) with a large knife attached to it and a brinjal in her hand.
chapterTitle: The Woman and Her Brother-in-Law of Kaikala

t: People in those days did not eat brinjal on the thirteenth day of the lunar month. You may still find the dictum in modern day almanacs: “It is forbidden to eat brinjals on the thirteenth day of the lunar month (trayodashii tithi).”
chapterTitle: The Woman and Her Brother-in-Law of Kaikala

t: Just as she was about to cut the brinjal, it occurred to her that it could be trayodashii that day. She asked her brother-in-law, “T́hákurpo, is it troyodashii today?”
chapterTitle: The Woman and Her Brother-in-Law of Kaikala

t: The man touched his hair and replied, “This is a vow for Bábá Táraknáth (another name of Lord Shiva).”
chapterTitle: The Woman and Her Brother-in-Law of Kaikala

t: His sister-in-law said, “I see, then shall I cut the brinjal?”
chapterTitle: The Woman and Her Brother-in-Law of Kaikala

t: He replied, “It is as Bábá Táraknáth wishes.”
chapterTitle: The Woman and Her Brother-in-Law of Kaikala

t: Since ancient times, a woman has respected her elder brother-in-law in the same manner as her father-in-law. Therefore, he was addressed with due honour as baŕa t́hákur or bat́t́hákur. However, it was the custom that he should not be touched.
There was an incident which happened in Mánád (Mahánád ( 1 )). Let me quickly narrate it.

The woman of the house said under her breath, “A thief... a thief is circling the house with a burglarʼs tool trying to break in... I know everything... but I must feign ignorance... clever that I am... I shall wait to see what happens.”
“Oh, I can hear the sound of the thief breaking in... I lie with eyes shut but know what he is up to. However, I shall keep mum... clever that I am... I shall wait and see.”
“Oh, he has entered the house... let me turn over to the other side and pretend to be fast asleep... I shall not open my eyes... I shall wait... clever that I am.”

“The thief has collected all valuable things... everything he tied up in a bundle... it is a big bundle... he cannot take it out through the hole he came in... I am indeed clever... I am waiting and waiting without making a sound.”

“How will he go out with the big bundle now?... rubbish dump to the right... bat́t́hákur to the left... both are untouchable... one has to take a bath if one touches them by mistake. Where will you go now, thief? To your right is the rubbish dump, to the left bat́t́hákur... what will you do now?”
You may not have heard about this incident for it happened a long, long time ago.

The wife of the third son of the Neugi (Neogi) family in Ámnán ( 1 ) was a very domineering woman. The wives of the other sons did not wield as much authority (possibly because their husbands earned less).

The dominant woman of the family thought up a clever ploy to turn the other wives out of the house. Her parents lived in Gopinagar. They were poor and somehow eked out a living. She brought all her family members from Gopinagar to Ámnán, including her nephews and nieces, servants, the pet cat and the canary in the cage. The situation at her in-lawʼs house became so impossible that the wives of the other brothers were forced to leave.

The dominant wife got her way. Even after one hundred years, the people of Ámnán tell each other – the wife of the third son of the Neogis brought droves of her own folks from her parentʼs place in Gopinagar which doubled the population of Ámnán.

Dundubhi does not only mean a large war trumpet. Somewhere in old Sanskrit literature, it has been used to mean a victory drum, a kettledrum as well as a war drum. Hence, dundubhi refers to any of these instruments. It can also mean a horn (shruṋgiká/viśáń ), another instrument. Viśáń is commonly called shingá in Bengali and tutru in the Auṋgiká dialect.
Have you heard the rhyme on sounding the tutru in Auṋgiká?

In those days, Shivchandra Báṋŕujye was a renowned man in Bhagalpur. The government of India had estimated the cost of constructing water works in Bhagalpur city to be two lakh rupees. It was announced that any generous person donating the full amount ( 1 ) would be rewarded with the title Mahárájá [a great king] by the government. The title of Rájá [king] would be bestowed on whomever donated one lakh rupees.

Shivchandra Báṋŕujye donated one lakh rupees. He was honoured with the title of Rájá by the government of India. He was a king without a kingdom, somewhat like Raja Rammohan Roy. The rural folks of Bhagalpur sang a rhyme in his name.
Ná d́hol ná d́hák tutru bájá,
Ná ráj ná pát́ Shivcandar rájá
[No tom-toms, no drums, sound of the tutru, No kingdom, no throne, but Shivchandra is king.]

You may have noticed that some cows are well-mannered and produce a good quantity of milk, but as soon as someone approaches them, they chase the person down and gore them. In some cases it can be fatal. This type of cow is called márkánd́á gái [aggressive cow] in some parts of Bihar. Even sheep and other domestic pets can be aggressive. Aggressive animals are usually those with horns. Aggressive animals are given to growling and fuming and rubbing their bodies against the wall when they have nothing to do.

According to psychologists, men and mostly women who are quarrelsome by nature rub their palms on the floor or wall when they are unable to find a reason for starting an altercation. There is a saying – you cannot clap with one hand, but these people are capable of doing that.
Animals cannot kick up a row on every pretext due to lack of intelligence, but human beings are different. Even without any apparent reason, they can start a quarrel.

There is a story that a certain quarrelsome gentleman in Dhanekhali – probably by the name Ranachandiranjan Sur ( 1 ) – did not find anyone to quarrel with one day. As long as his wife Kháńd́árńi [shrew] Devii was alive, he had no problem in starting a fight. At any time of the day or night, there was a worthy partner available in the same house. However, the departure of his wife for the other world put him in a fix. He had to find a suitable person these days to brawl with.

Ranachandi Sur decided to visit Uttarpara on that day to pick a quarrel. Uttarpara is a big place, and hence it would not be difficult to find a few persons to quarrel with. He ordered the man who tended his horse to -
Sájá ghoŕá, sájá ghoŕá, áj yábo otorpáŕá.
[Get the horse ready, I want to go to Uttarpara.]

Mr. Sur mounted his saddled horse and set out on his way. At that moment, Haru Biswas of Dhanekhali, with his dress pulled up to above the knees, was squatting on the road counting a cluster of bananas. He asked, “Why are you going to Uttarpara so early in the morning?”

That was enough to ignite Mr. Sur. He bared his teeth, made an ugly face, and like a wild boar, growled, “Why should any accursed rascal want to know that? I shall teach everyone a lesson, I shall challenge the whole world today. I shall define what a real row is. I shall show what even the trinity of gods could not do!” He called upon his saiis [caretaker of his horse] and said,
Báṋdh ghoŕá, báṋdh ghoŕá, peyechi koṋdoler goŕá.
[Rein in the horse, I have found a reason to brawl.]

The aggressive cows I was talking about are difficult to milk. Even men are frightened of them and women find it even more difficult to milk them. A regular milkman has to be called in to milk such cows.
Have you heard the story of the aggressive sheep? I shall narrate it briefly.

Once upon a time, three well-known men had gathered on the bathing ghát́ [landing platform] of Chandannagore. One was a man stricken with ringworm who hailed from Dádpur ( 2 ), another was a man with an eye inflammation from Chandanpur. The third was a bald man from the village of Takipur.

The three men were going to Kankinara on the other side of the river. The boatman said, “All three of you are respected gentlemen. I shall not accept any fare for ferrying you to the other side, but I have one condition. While on my boat, the one with ringworm should not scratch himself even once, the one with the eye infection should not rub his eyes, and the bald gentleman must not cover his head with wet cloth or soak his head with water.”

They agreed to the boatmanʼs condition. It was a cloudy day. A gentle breeze was blowing across a quiet river. They expected the journey to be comfortable. A little while later, a scorching sun beat down upon them. The man afflicted with ringworm was overwhelmed with the desire to scratch. He thought of an idea and said loudly to his fellow passengers, “What is the point in all of us keeping quiet when none of us is deaf and dumb by the grace of God? Why should we not give honour to the power of our speech? Friends, let us narrate tales, true stories, and cheer everyone up. That way the distance to Kankinara will seem much less.” After a slight pause, he said, “Let me begin first.”

“There were a number of sheep in our house. One of them was very aggressive. It used to chase and gore anyone who came close to it. When there was no one around, true to the nature of aggressive animals, it rubbed its body against the wall. Do you know how? Like this, like this” he said and he scratched himself hard.
Now it was the turn of the man with eye inflammation. He began, “We also had a number of sheep but none was aggressive. All of them were calm and had wonderful horns. What magnificent horns!”

He stretched both his arms as far as possible in front of his face, made fists and rotated his wrists round and round. He said, “The horns of the rams were like this, curved and twisted, curved and twisted and sharp,” and as he said this he brought his arms near his face, twirled his fists and rubbed his eyes viciously.

The bald man then took the opportunity. He said, “In my village at Takipur ( 3 ), no one had any sheep, but baldness was common in every household. About 99.9 percent of the men in the village were bald (indralupti in Sanskrit). The bald patches were large, oily and sticky to the touch. In short, not only were they charming, but every observer was carried away by their beauty.”

He continued, “Potato is a major crop in Dhanekhali area. We did not keep sheep as pets because they dig up and eat the potatoes in the field. There were a number of ponds in our village with young, good quality fish, especially of the rui, kátlá and mrgel (mirik in western Ráŕh) variety. Rudd fish (kálibáus in western Ráŕh) was particularly good. The best district in Ráŕh is Hooghly, of which the best village is Takipur where our pond surrounded by palm trees is the best. Some rui fish in it are huge – as large as twenty buffaloes put together. They are so big... oh, how shall I show you the size! This is the problem... they were truly large... very large... as large as...” So saying, he extended his hands sideways and scooped up some water. “Sooo big... and do you know how wide they are?” As he said that he revolved his hands in a half-circle and sprinkled the water on his bald pate. He said, “So wide ... so wide ...” Finally, he brought his arms near his head and slapped it with the open palms and said, “Have you now got a measure of how wide they were?” Thus he repeated the description of the fishʼs size a few times, collecting water each time while explaining the length and soaked his head thoroughly while he gestured to show its width.
When his glabrous crown was cooled, he changed the song he had been humming for some time. Earlier, he was singing:
Telálo cyát́álo t́áke legeche jáṋjhálo roder háoyá.
[The stinging rays of the sun have assailed this oily, sticky, bald head.]
He changed his song now, to:
Tumi sushital tumi suvimal Gauṋgár jal tumi shiital.
[Oh, the water of Ganga! you are pleasant and cool, you are chilly.]
So the three men cleverly realised their ends. The appreciative boatman looked at them in a bewildered way.
Now you know the tale of the aggressive sheep.

Have you heard of this mythological story of yore? Kashyap, the great sage, had two wives – Kadru and Binata. Once, Kadru laid many eggs while Binata laid only two. Each of Kadruʼs eggs hatched one species of snake. (That is why kadruja also means snake and káshyapeya means snake as well, along with its many other meanings.)

However, Binataʼs eggs did not hatch. Finding her co-wife happy and resplendent with children, Binata was desperate with envy. She smashed one of her eggs in frustration. It had not matured yet. The red yolk was still crimson and it turned into a fiery ball. The effulgent man who emerged from it rebuked his mother, “You have made a big blunder by breaking the egg prematurely. I shall not stay with you.” He left her and went to the Sun.

The Sun said, “Come, do stay with me. I never destroy anything before its time. I do everything at the right time.” Then he added, “I hereby name you Arun. You will be the charioteer of my chariot pulled by seven horses (VIBGYOR).”
According to mythology, the crimson red colour which engulfs the eastern sky at the break of dawn is Arun, the Sunʼs charioteer.

Binata had learnt her lesson. She waited for the second egg to reach maturity. In due course, a giant bird with a needle-sharp beak was hatched. The bird bowed and, touching the feet of his mother, said, “It is in my nature to fly. I cannot be tied down to a perch (dṋáŕ ( 1 )) at home. I shall move out.”

The bird kept flying and flying beyond the atmosphere to the unknown blue of the azure sky. It reached Vaekunt́ha, the land of Viśńu. It said to Viśńu, “O Lord Viśńu, you are a dynamic force. You never remain static. I too am not born to remain static. It is in my nature to fly. So please make me your mount.” Thus the bird became Viśńuʼs mount. Viśńu named it Garud́a.

The snake is the sworn enemy of human beings and other creatures. Just as snakes (sáp) are afraid of humans, so also humans are afraid of snakes. Generally, a non-venomous snake does not carry a circular mark (cakra) on its hood. However, a venomous snake is never without this mark, though there are a few exceptions.
In indigenous Bengali, a non-venomous snake is called a d́hoṋŕá. I shall tell you about it later.
Non-venomous snakes like the citi and hele are fundamentally of the d́hoṋŕá species. In any case, men are extremely scared of venomous snakes. I recall an incident.
Once, a clever man wanted to make fun of a blind man. He exclaimed, “ Oh blind man! What a snake there is!”
The blind man said, “Oh, what a fearful cakra on its hood!”
The other man feigned ignorance, “Is that so! Where is it?”
The blind man said, “You said so yourself, did you not, rascal?”

Once upon a time, it was a common belief among people that a young childʼs lifespan could be enhanced and evil spirits warded off if a coloured thread (ghunsi) was worn around the childʼs waist. They strongly believed that such a lucky charm ferreted out evil forces and destroyed them.

In this connection, I recollect an old story. A very rich but miserly person in Burdwan went to buy a ghunsi for his son in Ranigunj market. He visited seven hundred shops but did not find a suitable lucky charm. Some he found not to his liking and for others, the price was too high.
In one shop he asked the price of a ghunsi. The shopkeeper said, “Two for one paisa.” The man moved to another shop and asked, “How much is yours?”
“One paisa for two,” replied the shopkeeper.
“Make it four,” said the man. “You must give me a bargain offer which you do not give others. Why not give it cheaply to me and make up the loss from other buyers! Just see what a poor man I am.”

After some haggling, the shopkeeper agreed to sell him three for one paisa. However, the buyer was still not satisfied. He thought the price too high. He said, “Will these last for a long time? You are making a big profit out of me all right, but these must last long.”

The shopkeeper said, “Do not worry about it, sir. My ghunsis are very lucky. The thread will not break even when your son eventually dies. It will remain intact tied to his waist. So lucky are my charms!”

Talking of a ghunsi, I am reminded of the story of a hat. Once, a farmer of noble birth earned ready cash from selling jute and went to the city with the money to buy a stylish hat. He checked seven thousand hats, selected one and asked, “Will this hat last long?”
The shopkeeper replied, “Of course sir, it will last for years.”
“How many years, approximately?”
“It will last till even when your jánájá [funeral rites] ( 1 )is being performed.”
This assurance made the buyer exceedingly happy. He asked the price.
“One rupee four annas, sir.”
“Make it a rupee,” said the customer.
“Look sir, why donʼt you buy a málshá [small earthen basin] from some shop. It will serve you two purposes. You can use it for drinking water. You may also put it on your head like a hat.”
I do not know what the farmer did with the shopkeeperʼs advice.

By then night had set in. Nothing could be seen. The prince was waiting for the auspicious hour before sunrise known as Bráhma Muhúrta ( 1 ). Just at Bráhma Muhúrta, he thought about God and set off towards his destination. And, would you believe, after some time he saw a huge palm tree. A quilt, mattress, cot, bed, table, jug, glass, every household article, were on top of the tree, and yet the householder himself was absent. And, would you believe, beside it the prince saw a real chocolate tree. He thought, “I can eat chocolates any day so whatʼs the use of climbing up that tree. Instead Iʼll walk on a little further.”

After going a little distance he saw an áshke cake tree (áshke pit́he) ( 2 ). Quite a large number of broken and unbroken ashke cakes were lying scattered here and there on the ground under the tree. Abhijit was a clever boy. Seeing the debris, he guessed that some kind of incident must have taken place there.

Abhijit decided to keep watch on that tree. Normally a tiger, due to greed, will continuously move around that very spot where it previously had the good luck to catch itʼs prey. If anyone had snatched Madhumita away from this place, that person was likely to return again.

From where he was sitting, Abhijit caught sight of a fried-cake tree (bhájá pit́he). He quickly went and scaled the tree and even ate one or two fried cakes. The cakes were delightfully tasty. They were made of the best golden Nadia [District] lentils and filled with coconut, and steaming hot as if straight from the pan.
While sitting there he ate a few more cakes and thought: “If I go and sit on that tree in front, Iʼll be able to keep a good watch on the áshke cake tree.”

He did just that. He went and sat on top of that large tree, which was a huge puli cake tree. The inside of each puli cake (puli pit́he) was filled with condensed milk, and treacle [syrup made of date palm raw sugar] was dripping from the sides of those steaming hot cakes... drip... drip... drip.
While sitting on the tree, Abhijit ate cakes and kept watch on the áshke cake tree. Just then, he caught sight of a cow-ghost standing under his puli-cake tree.
Abhijit asked, “Sister ghost, sister ghost, would you like to eat a cake?”
The cow-ghost said: “No thank you. Iʼve just had a full meal of cattle-fodder. Therefore I wonʼt eat cakes just now, thank you. Iʼve simply come to remind you about something.”
Abhijit asked, “About what? About what? Tell me... Tell me!”
The cow-ghost said: “Ekanoŕe ghost [one-legged ghost] lives on that palm tree over there. Heʼs a most civilized fellow, most gentle, and most educated.”
Abhijit asked: “Whatʼs his full name?”
The cow-ghost said: “His full name is Mr. Ekanoŕe Bhattacharya, MA, LLB, D. Litt., M. Comm., Doctor of Poetry, Sánkhya Philosophy and Grammar and Master of Logic.”
The cow-ghost added: “If he comes back here, donʼt waste any time in making friends with him. Heʼs a very benevolent person.”
Abhijit asked, “Where has he gone now?”

The cow-ghost said: “He has perhaps gone to make arrangements for his fatherʼs last rites. Because, for the last few days, I have seen a Brahmadaetya [a degenerated high-caste ghost] priest nagging him with a long list of different things.”
Abhijit asked, “Why? Why? ... For what purpose?”

The cow-ghost replied: “After all, it is the last rites of a ghostʼs father, you know! For that so many things are required, so much money is needed. It is for that very reason that the Brahmdaetya was nagging around him with a long list.”
Abhijit said, “Oh, I see. Then the last rites of a ghostʼs father is quite a costly affair?”

The cow-ghost said, “Yes, extremely expensive. You know, only sinful people become ghosts after death and, if they donʼt spend a lot of money on the last rites, they wonʼt be able to go to heaven. Thatʼs why the poor ghosts have to stay down in hell and rot there. Tell me, whoʼs going to spend such a large sum on them for their last rites?”
Abhijit asked, “So where has he gone now?”

The cow-ghost replied, “Heʼs most probably gone to Benaras ( 3 ) to perform the last rites. In order to make the necessary arrangements, the poor man was obliged to incur a huge financial debt. Ekanoŕe even had to pawn the ladder he used for climbing into his tree to purchase the items required for the last rites. Thatʼs why, even at such an age, he now has to scale the tree like a monkey. I must be going now. Donʼt forget, prince, that you should not waste any time in making friends with Ekanoŕe.”
Just as the cow-ghost was about to leave, Abhijit noticed a huge raven flying over his head. Surprisingly enough, it wasnʼt holding even a single cake in its beak.
Abhijit enquired, “Oh, sister cow-ghost, why isnʼt that raven eating any cakes? And why is he making that strange type of kor kor sound?”
The cow-ghost replied, “Thatʼs a mangosteen ( 4 ) (gáb) eating raven; now heʼs become a ghost.”
Abhijit asked, “Whatʼs a mangosteen eating raven? I have never heard of such a thing!”

The cow-ghost said, “In that case, listen to his story. Once-upon-a-time there was a raven who was extremely greedy. One day, while hitting at a large mangosteen fruit with his beak, he happened to swallow it. Actually, he ate it out of intense greed but found to his dismay that his condition was just like a snake who had eaten a musk-rat ( 5 ). Neither could he swallow it, nor could he throw it up. Oh, what terrible pain he was in! Then the raven moved throughout the whole universe; up to the heavens, across the earth, down to the underworld, in search of a doctor who would be able to save him by cutting the mangosteen in his throat into pieces. He cried out with great difficulty:
Gáb taláte ár yáboná
Gáb phal ár kháboná.
[To the mangosteen I will never go again. The mangosteen I will never eat again.]

“All the worldʼs ayurvedic doctors knew that the raven was voraciously greedy and therefore they all decided: 'First of all let him rectify himself and only then will we cut up the fruit.ʼ Seeing his profuse weeping, an elderly ayurvedic doctor felt sorry for him. He said: 'Come here, raven, letʼs see what I can do for you. But you will have to promise me that you will never indulge in such things again.́

“The raven said, 'Respected doctor, if you think I will, you must be mad. Here I am, prostrating before you, touching your feet with the ten claws of my feet and vowing that I will never again eat mangosteen in my life.ʼ
“And, weeping, he further said:
Gáb taláte ár yáboná
Gáb phal ár kháboná.
[To the mangosteen I will never go again. The mangosteen I will never eat again.]

“Then the respected doctor, after sterilizing his sharp knife in a flame, cut the mangosteen stuck in the throat into four pieces. The raven heaved a sigh of relief. Then he flew to a mangosteen tree and greedily gulped down the four pieces of mangosteen. And then said to the ayurvedic doctor:
Gáb kháboná khábo kii?
Gáber matan ache kii?
[If I donʼt eat mangosteen what else will I eat? What else is there except mangosteen to eat?]

“Saying this, he flew off. And then, after a few days, he choked himself on a mangosteen stuck in his throat and died. He was extraordinarily greedy. Thatʼs why you see him now flying in the sky as a raven ghost. He doesnʼt touch anything else except mangosteen. Only one sound comes out of his throat: ‘g-á-á-á-b... [Mangostee-ee-een].’ Look, heʼs still making that sound.”
Abhijit said, “Itʼs true, heʼs making that sound while flying around.” And he asked: “And for how long will he have to go on making that sound?”
The cow-ghost said, “He will have to continue until the day comes when he is set free from the ghost life.”
The cow-ghost left in a leisurely manner.
Again, Abhijit concentrated on the cakes. While nibbling at the puli cakes he remembered what he had heard just the day before yesterday while sitting in his grandmotherʼs lap:
Kálekále katai halo
Pulipit́her nyáj gajálo.
[In the course of years strange things happen The puli cakes grow tails ( 6 ).]
But there werenʼt any tails on these puli cakes. Just then, suddenly, a giant figure of a ghost came and stood beside him.
Abhijit said, “Are you Brother Ekanoŕe?”
Ekanoŕe replied, “Yes.”
Abhijit asked, “Whereʼs Mrs. Ekanoŕe?”
Just then Mrs. Fish-Eating ghost came running up to them in great haste. She said, “Here I am, prince, is there any work you want me to do? Tell me if there is and I will do it straight away.”
Abhijit said, “No I donʼt have any work for you. I was only making enquiries about you because you are our sister-in-law, thatʼs why.”
Abhijit asked Ekanoŕe, “Brother, have you just returned after performing your fatherʼs last rites?”
Ekanoŕe said, “I went to Benaras for that purpose. I had to buy many things as per the dictates of the Brahmadaetyaʼs huge list.”

He added, “The more gifts given to the priest, the higher my fatherʼs ascent into heaven will be. Therefore, I had to incur a debt in order to properly arrange everything. But now the priest at Benaras has greatly inconvenienced me. According to him this month is an inauspicious one and so the last rites wonʼt be possible. Now, they can only take place in a monthʼs time. He asserts that this is the convention of the ghostsʼ world.”
Abhijit said, “I understand all that and yet seeing your difficult situation I feel very distressed.”

Ekanoŕe said, “You are a very good boy, and thatʼs why you feel pain on seeing the suffering of others. But not everyone is like that. Take my case, for example. I have studied a lot, taught in a college and a school of Sanskrit, and practised a little ayurvedic medicine. In those days I used to manufacture medicine of world-wide repute in my ayurvedic laboratory. There I made 'palatial-house powderʼ (brhat att́áliká curńa) and ‘giant elephant and gold compounded tablets’ (svarńaghatita subrhat hastii bhasma vatiká), and thousands upon thousands of them were sold each month. Now, you see, when success goes to oneʼs head, one loses compassion for oneʼs fellow men. That, indeed, happened to me. I took to adulterating my products. And then, in course of time, I lost everything. Today I am penniless, destitute, the scum of the earth. Dear prince, I have committed many sins and, as a result, have become Ekánoŕe ghost, and have had to set up house in the palm tree. Until these sins are neutralized by virtuous deeds, I wonʼt have peace of mind. Even now I think, twenty-four hours a day I think, in what way I may atone for these sins. Whenever I get the opportunity I try my best to do good to others. Always keep in mind, prince, that a bad deed will never have good results, and a good deed will never have bad results.”
The prince listened with rapt attention and, seeing Ekanoreʼs repentant nature, his eyes filled with tears. He said, “Iʼve heard many people admiring you.”
Ekanoŕe said, “Who?”
Abhijit said, “The cow-ghost.”
Ekanoŕe said, “The cow-ghost is a really good lady. She is fond of everyone. When she was alive she used to give 10,000 kilos of condensed milk daily.”
The prince exclaimed, “Condensed milk! Are you serious?”

Ekanoŕe said, “Yes, condensed milk. I really mean it. Other cows give milk when they are milked, but she used to give condensed milk sometimes freshly clotted, sometimes steaming, sometimes hot. You canʼt imagine how tasty and palatable it was. I can clearly remember, prince, that we once had such a severely cold winter that everything was quickly frozen, and even the waters of the river Ganges turned into ice. I wanted to take the launch from Chinsurah fish market to Naihati [24 Parganas District]. However, the launch service had stopped. After all, you canʼt expect a launch to travel over ice. As I wasnʼt one to be easily deterred, I drove over the ice of the Ganges on a motorcycle and in just one minute reached Naihati. There was no need to drive over the ice to get to Howrah from Calcutta as thereʼs a bridge. But a number of times I amused myself by driving up as far as Salkia Bandhaghat [in Howrah District] from Ahiritola [in Kolkata]. Oh, what a thrilling experience. Just thinking about it makes me jump with joy. Oh yes, let me return to what I was talking about. For some days during that very winter I milked the cow. On milking her I was astonished: 'My goodness, what happened to the condensed milk?ʼ It had turned to ice-cream. After that, for fifteen days at a stretch ice-cream came out of the cowʼs udder. That season I sold ice-cream and pocketed 500,000 rupees.”

We got the word cávi from Portuguese language. In Portuguese, cha is pronounced somewhat like sha. I heard both the Portuguese and Spanish people pronounce cávi shábi. Currently this word cávi is widely used both in Bengal and in the whole of North India. Surprisingly, even 450 years ago no one in this country was familiar with this word. In North India cávi used to be called kuiṋjii and in Bengal kát́hi. Even today some people in Ráŕh call tálá-cavi [ lock and key] kulup-kát́hi. Even those who habitually say cavi call it cávi-kát́hi. Once the word kuiṋjii was frequently used in Urdu. Now its influence is declining. There goes an Urdu story like this:
One candidate was not at all studious but very humorous. On every page of the answer paper, he wrote,
Házáro kii kismat tere háṋtho me hae
Agar pás kará deiṋ to kyá bát hae.
[The fate of thousands of candidates is in your hand. Whatʼs the harm if you help them pass the exam?]
The examiner was even more humorous. At each place where the boy had written the above lines, he wrote in reply,
kitávoṋ kii kuiṋjii tere hátho meṋ hyáy
Agar yád kar leṋ to kyá bát hyáy?
[The cávi of the book is in Your hand. Whatʼs the harm if you memorize the book?]
